What Three Years of Poor Financial Habits Taught Me

I started working at the age of 24, but it took me until I was 27 to finally build meaningful savings. Looking back, I realized that for nearly three years,most of my income disappeared without leaving much behind.

The problem was not necessarily how much I earned. It was how I managed what Iearned. Five financial habits repeatedly worked against me, and learning torecognize them completely changed the way I think about money.

Here are five financial habits I wish I had avoided from the beginning.

1. Living Above Your Means

Living above your means simply means spending more than your income canreasonably support. The concept sounds obvious, but actually avoiding it canbe surprisingly difficult—especially when a paycheck arrives and suddenlyeverything feels affordable.

When I first started earning my own money, I treated my salary asfree money. After years of depending on my parents, having my ownincome felt like having unlimited freedom.

I started buying things because my friends had them, checking out productsimpulsively, and spending money on short-term entertainment. Eventually, theentire paycheck could disappear before I even realized where it went.

The problem became even more obvious when I saw people around me buying cars,motorcycles, and expensive gadgets. I realized that constantly trying to keepup with other people's lifestyles could easily become a long-term financialtrap.

The rule that helped me:

  • I stopped buying expensive things unless I could comfortably afford themwithout putting my finances under pressure.
  • One personal rule I experimented with was having roughly 10 times the priceof a non-essential purchase already saved. For example, if I wanted aRp20 million phone, I would want around Rp200 million in savings first.
  • I also started waiting one to three weeks before making expensive purchases.If I still wanted the item after the waiting period, I would reconsider itmore rationally.

This simple delay eliminated many impulse purchases. Most of the time, Ieventually realized that I wanted the excitement of buying something—notnecessarily the thing itself.

2. Saving Whatever Is Left

My old strategy was simple: get paid, spend the money, and save whateverremained at the end of the month.

The problem was that there was almost never anything meaningful left.Unexpected expenses, food, entertainment, online shopping, and small dailypurchases gradually consumed the money.

Eventually, I realized that saving could not be something I did only when itwas convenient. It needed to become a priority.

The approach that worked better:

  • Estimate my essential monthly living expenses first.
  • Decide how much I wanted to save.
  • Move the savings into a separate account immediately after payday.
  • Use the remaining money for everyday expenses.

For example, if my monthly income were Rp10 million and my essentialexpenses were approximately Rp5.5 million, I could decide to move theremaining Rp4.5 million into savings at the beginning of the month ratherthan waiting until the end.

Step Example Purpose
Estimate living expenses Rp5.5 million/month Know the amount needed for daily life
Save first Rp4.5 million Make saving a priority
Spend what remains Rp5.5 million Keep everyday spending within a limit

There is also a psychological advantage to this approach. Once money hasalready been moved into a separate savings account, I become less likely totreat it as available spending money.

In other words: don't save what is left after spending. Spend what isleft after saving.

3. Keeping All Your Money in One Account

Another mistake I made was putting everything into a single bank account.Spending money, savings, and emergency funds all looked like one big balance.

That created a dangerous illusion: if the account showed a large balance,I felt like I had plenty of money to spend—even though some of that moneywas actually meant for the future.

My solution: separate the money by purpose.

  • Spending account: money for everyday expenses.
  • Savings/investment account: money intended for longer-termgoals.
  • Emergency fund: money reserved for genuine unexpectedsituations.

The exact number of accounts is not important. What matters is creating aclear boundary between money that is available to spend and money that hasanother purpose.

Sometimes good financial management is less about having incredibleself-control and more about designing your environment so that bad decisionsbecome harder to make.

4. Wanting to Get Rich Too Quickly

One of the most expensive lessons I learned was that the desire to becomewealthy quickly can make people ignore obvious warning signs.

I once lost tens of millions of rupiah after putting money into an MLM-styleinvestment opportunity that promised returns of around 20% per month.Several months later, the money was gone.

Looking back, the promised returns should have been a major warning sign.I was so attracted to the possibility of making money quickly that I paidless attention to the risks.

Scams can take many forms. They may involve investments, businesses,cryptocurrencies, online platforms, or even people we know personally.The presentation changes, but the underlying psychological tricks can remainsurprisingly similar.

Some lessons I took from the experience:

  • Be extremely skeptical of unusually high or guaranteed returns.
  • Never assume an opportunity is safe simply because someone you knowrecommends it.
  • Don't invest money you cannot afford to lose without understanding therisks.
  • Research how the business actually makes money instead of focusing onlyon testimonials and success stories.
  • Don't assume you are smarter than the people trying to persuade you.

Building wealth can certainly happen quickly in some circumstances, butsustainable wealth generally requires some combination of valuable skills,disciplined saving, reasonable risk-taking, time, and sometimes a bit ofluck.

5. Ignoring Opportunity Cost

Money is not the only resource we spend. We also spend time, energy,attention, and opportunities.

This is where the idea of opportunity cost becomes useful.Whenever we choose one option, we are also giving up the benefits we couldhave received from another option.

For example, spending four hours scrolling through short-form videos meansthose four hours cannot simultaneously be spent learning programming,studying mathematics, practicing English, exercising, or working on apersonal project.

The same applies to money. Spending Rp1 million on something today meansthat same Rp1 million cannot be used for another purpose.

Before making a decision, I now try to ask:

  • What am I gaining from this?
  • What am I giving up?
  • Is what I am gaining worth the opportunity I am sacrificing?

This doesn't mean every minute has to be productive. Rest, entertainment,hobbies, and spending money on things we enjoy are all legitimate parts oflife.

The important thing is to spend those resources intentionally rather thanautomatically.

What I Learned

None of these ideas are particularly revolutionary. Spend less than youearn. Save consistently. Avoid suspicious investments. Think about thefuture.

The difficult part is not understanding these principles. The difficultpart is actually following them when temptation, social pressure, andshort-term gratification get involved.

I learned these lessons through mistakes that cost me both time and money.If sharing my experience helps someone recognize the same mistakes beforemaking them, then those experiences were at least useful for something.

Personal finance is ultimately less about finding a secret formula forgetting rich and more about consistently making better decisions with theresources you already have.
